items.e: To concede is to admit that someone else is right, which is what "had to" signals here; to deny or to insist that she was right would mean he never gave in.

items.e: Sincere means truly meant, which matches the clue that she really meant it; a sarcastic apology is one that is not meant at all.

items.e: The grin that gives him away shows he got the cupcake by quiet trickery, which is what sly means; honest is the opposite, gracious describes warm manners, and someone who is puzzled has not just pulled off a trick.

items.e: Claiming only an extra hour rather than changing the world keeps her claims small and unexaggerated, which is what modest means here; boastful and grand describe exactly the big claims she avoids, and her careful wording is the opposite of reckless.
items.q: The inventor's claims were ______: she said the new battery might last an hour longer, not that it would change the world.

items.e: Standing by a friend when everyone else turns away is faithfulness, which is what loyal means; the sentence is not about bragging, about being liked by the crowd, or about running out of patience.
items.q: When the rest of the team stopped speaking to Priya after the missed penalty, Dana walked home with her as she always had; nobody who knew Dana was surprised at how ______ she was.

items.e: “Stung” rules out gentle and tactful, and the quoted remark names two specific faults, which rules out vague; blunt means honest in a way that spares no feelings.
items.q: His advice was accurate but so ______ that it stung: “Your essay is dull, and you never checked the spelling.”

items.e: Making a card and clapping for someone who drove two hours unasked is a show of thanks, which is what grateful means; annoyance and indifference would show no thanks at all, and nothing about the drive puzzles them.
items.q: Nobody had asked Mr. Odile to drive two hours with the costumes the cast had forgotten, and the cast was so ______ that they made him a card and clapped when he walked in.

items.e: A minute of silence that makes small children go still is grave and dignified, which rules out festive, playful, and casual.
items.q: The assembly opened with a ______ minute of silence for the school's founder, and even the youngest students stopped fidgeting.

items.e: “Feeling understood rather than scolded” rules out severe and mocking, and indifference would leave him feeling nothing; sympathetic means sharing in how someone else feels.

items.e: She is smiling and speaking fondly of what she misses, which rules out bitter and anxious; nothing is being waited for, so not impatient. Nostalgic is exactly this fond longing for the past.
items.q: The box of old camp photographs left Grandma smiling and ______, saying again and again how much she missed those summers by the lake.

items.e: Falling silent and mumbling at the end of a long hike shows worn-out tiredness, which is what weary means; a cheerful or playful hiker would still be talking, and nothing on the trail has alarmed her.
items.q: By the last mile of the hike Ana had stopped chattering altogether, and her answers came out in a ______ mumble.

items.e: A boastful person keeps announcing how good he is; complaining, fear, and generosity are unrelated traits.
items.q: BOASTFUL most nearly means:

items.e: Gracious describes warm good manners, the direct opposite of coldly rude, and it has nothing to do with confusion or humor.

items.e: Resentful is the sour anger left behind by treatment you think was unfair; gratitude is its opposite, and eagerness and puzzlement are not anger.
items.q: RESENTFUL most nearly means:

items.e: Melancholy is a low, lingering sadness, so humor, energy, and alertness all miss it.
items.q: MELANCHOLY most nearly means:

items.e: Grim describes something stern and cheerless; hopeful, silly, and welcoming are all the opposite in feeling.
items.q: GRIM most nearly means:

items.e: Apologetic means showing that you regret something you did; pride, anger, and curiosity carry no regret.

items.e: Scorn is contempt, so scornful means treating something as beneath you — the opposite of admiring, and unrelated to helpfulness or uncertainty.

items.e: Defiant means openly standing against an order, the opposite of obedient; amusement and gratitude are different feelings entirely.
items.q: DEFIANT most nearly means:

items.e: She insists on sharing the credit, which rules out smug, and insisting aloud is not timid; she plainly cares, so not indifferent. Humble means not thinking too highly of yourself.
items.q: Though the whole town praised her invention, Maya stayed ______, insisting that her science teacher deserved as much credit as she did.

items.e: Reminding everyone “yet again” of his own correct prediction is self-satisfied, not gracious; he is neither sorry (apologetic) nor worried (anxious) after winning.
items.q: After the win, Trent's grin was ______, and he reminded everyone yet again that he had predicted the score exactly.

items.e: Knocking pencils down harms nobody, so vicious (cruel) is far too strong; she is causing trouble, so not obedient, and darting off tail-high is not timid. Mischievous means playfully naughty.
items.q: The kitten's ______ streak showed the moment she batted every pencil off the desk and darted away with her tail high.

items.e: He encourages the team, which rules out gloomy and furious, and “still theirs for the taking” shows he is sure rather than uncertain; optimistic means expecting things to turn out well.
items.q: Two goals behind at half time, Coach stayed ______, telling the players the comeback was still theirs for the taking.

items.e: Seeing his name after expecting the worst lifts a weight off him, which is what relieved means; alarm, annoyance, and disappointment would all follow bad news, not good.
items.q: Ravi had been certain he had failed the audition, so when the cast list went up with his name on it, he sat down on the steps looking utterly ______.

items.e: “Rather than saying it was ugly” and the praise that comes first rule out blunt and rude, and she says nothing about herself, so not boastful; tactful means honest without wounding.
items.q: Rather than saying the painting was ugly, Nina gave a ______ reply, praising its colors before suggesting one change.

items.e: He seeks Nora out for petting, so he is not indifferent, and resting his head in her lap shows trust, which rules out hostile and fearful; affectionate means showing fondness.
items.q: The old dog was ______, nudging Nora's hand until she petted him and then settling his head in her lap.

items.e: Being “certain the news would be bad” is worry, not boredom, and the sleeve-chewing and clock-watching rule out relaxed and delighted; anxious means uneasy about what is coming.
items.q: With the results due any minute, Dev chewed his sleeve and kept checking the clock; he was plainly ______, certain the news would be bad.

items.e: Listing every flaw and praising almost nothing rules out admiring and cheerful, and the word “sharply” rules out neutral; critical here means fault-finding.
items.q: The review was sharply ______, listing every flaw in the play and praising almost nothing.

c: the power to decide for yourself
a rule that must always be followed
items.e: When a trip is “left to the principal's discretion,” she has the power to decide; a rule that must be followed is the opposite of leaving a choice to someone.
items.q: DISCRETION most nearly means:

c: agreed to by every single member
decided by one person in charge
put off until a later meeting
items.e: A unanimous vote is one in which everyone agrees. The look-alike word is anonymous, which means the name is not known.
items.q: UNANIMOUS most nearly means:

c: acting in a sneaky, guilty way
items.e: A conspicuous stain is one everyone sees at once. Suspicious (sneaky) and conscientious (careful) are the two look-alike words that do not mean the same thing.
items.q: CONSPICUOUS most nearly means:

items.e: A benign remark or a benign old dog does no harm; none of the other choices carries the idea of harmlessness.
items.q: BENIGN most nearly means:

c: a hard spot to get out of
a promise made in front of a crowd
a guess about what will happen next
a long delay before an event
items.e: Being locked out in the rain with no phone is a predicament — a situation you cannot easily escape. The look-alike word is prediction, a guess about the future.
items.q: PREDICAMENT most nearly means:

c: to remind someone of a chore
to plan carefully for next year
to talk fondly about times gone by
items.e: To reminisce is to look back and share memories, the way grandparents do about their childhood; reminding, apologizing, and planning all point at the present or future.
items.q: REMINISCE most nearly means:

c: to get smaller little by little
items.e: Interest that wanes fades bit by bit, the way a waning moon shrinks each night; its partner word wax means to grow.
items.q: WANE most nearly means:

c: spoken in a very loud voice
having to do with books and authors
taking words in their exact meaning
items.e: The literal meaning of “raining cats and dogs” would be actual animals falling from the sky. Literary, the look-alike word, is about books.
items.q: LITERAL most nearly means:

items.e: In “cost was a subordinate concern,” cost mattered less than the main issue; something subordinate ranks below, never above or equal.
items.q: SUBORDINATE most nearly means:

c: spread out over a wide area
items.e: A compact kitchen fits everything into a small area; compact says nothing about softness, single use, or wide spread.
items.q: COMPACT most nearly means:

items.e: Capital is the money and resources needed to start or run a business, which is exactly what the ovens, rent, and flour require.
items.q: Starting a bakery takes more ______ than most people expect: ovens, rent, and flour must all be paid for before the first loaf is sold.

items.e: Here content means what is inside the essay — the ideas and the evidence — rather than how much was written (volume); this is a different meaning from “content with her meal,” which means satisfied.
items.q: Mr. Alvarez graded the ______ of each essay — the ideas and the evidence — rather than the neatness of the handwriting.

items.e: A term is a word or expression used for something — a different meaning from a school term or the terms of a contract.
items.q: Our science teacher wrote the ______ “habitat” on the board and asked us to explain what it names.

items.e: A volume is one book of a set; “the one covering A through C” rules out the loudness and the amount meanings.
items.q: Grandma keeps the first ______ of the old encyclopedia, the one covering A through C, beside her chair.

items.e: To render assistance is to give it, which is exactly what delivering water and blankets describes; refusing or suspending help would mean the opposite, and to eradicate something is to wipe it out completely.
items.q: When the storm knocked out the power, the fire department ______ assistance to every family on the block, delivering water and blankets before midnight.

items.e: A grant is a sum of money given for a purpose; “used the money” shows this is the noun, not the verb “to grant permission.”
items.q: The museum applied for a ______ from the city and used the money to repair its leaking roof.

items.e: To charter a boat or a bus is to hire it for private use — the verb sense, not the city charter that is a founding document.
items.q: Because no ferry ran on Sundays, the team had to ______ a boat to reach the island for the tournament.

items.e: The numbers fall from 400 to 50, so decline here means to go steadily down, not to turn down an invitation.
items.q: Ticket sales began to ______ in the third week, dropping from four hundred a night to barely fifty.

items.e: Tender here means gentle and kind, which is what calms the kitten; the sore-to-the-touch meaning of tender would not describe a voice.
items.q: The vet spoke in a ______ voice and moved slowly, and the frightened kitten stopped shaking.

items.e: Static is the crackling noise that blocks a radio signal — a noun, and a different meaning from static as “not changing.”
items.q: The old radio crackled with so much ______ that we could not make out a single word of the weather report.

c: to take unfair advantage of someone
items.e: An employer who exploits workers profits from them by paying unfairly; praising, repairing, and handing over involve no unfair use.
items.q: EXPLOIT most nearly means:

c: to wait for someone else to act
to try hard over a long time
items.e: To strive for a goal is to keep making real effort toward it; each of the other choices describes not making that effort.
items.q: STRIVE most nearly means:

c: a talent a person is born with
a piece of unexpected good luck
items.e: The discipline to practice every day is trained control over your own behavior, not a mood, a natural gift, or luck.
items.q: DISCIPLINE most nearly means:

c: polite and quiet in a crowd
items.e: A feisty puppy barks boldly at a much larger dog — full of spirit and unwilling to back down.
items.q: FEISTY most nearly means:

items.e: A prompt reply arrives right away, so prompt is about speed; care, repetition, and group size are different ideas.
items.q: PROMPT most nearly means:

c: to grow and care for over time
to cut down and clear away
items.e: Farmers cultivate crops and people cultivate friendships — both mean tending something so it develops; cutting down is closer to the opposite.
items.q: CULTIVATE most nearly means:

c: built a very long time ago
having to do with the home
items.e: Domestic chores are household chores and a domestic animal is one kept at home; the other choices all point away from the home.
items.q: DOMESTIC most nearly means:

c: to strike back after being harmed
to go back and fetch something
to say sorry and make peace
items.e: A team that trips a player after being tripped retaliates. Retrieve (fetch) and retreat (pull back) are the look-alike words.
items.q: RETALIATE most nearly means:

items.e: “Trained every morning anyway” shows she held firmly to her purpose, which is what resolute means; the other three say nothing about determination.
items.q: Two coaches told Nadia the record was out of reach, but she remained ______ and trained every morning anyway.

items.e: Tangible proof is solid evidence you can touch or point to, which is exactly what the missing photograph and footprint would have been.
items.q: The class had plenty of theories about the missing mascot but no ______ proof — no photograph, no footprint, nothing they could point to.

items.e: To stifle something is to smother or hold it back, and a rule that punishes every mistake crushes the curiosity the teacher wants; cultivating curiosity would grow it instead, exploiting means using something unfairly for your own gain, and nothing here is being measured.
items.q: A classroom rule that punishes every mistake can ______ the very curiosity the teacher hopes to build.

items.e: Treacherous here means disloyal — betraying the trust placed in him — a different sense from a treacherous mountain road. Conspicuous is ruled out by “quietly.”
items.q: The general finally learned that his most trusted messenger had been ______ all along, quietly carrying the battle plans to the enemy.

items.e: Something dubious is doubtful and not to be trusted, which is how an offer that seems too good to be true sounds; the other three say nothing about doubt.
items.q: The offer sounded ______ to Mom: a free bicycle for anyone who simply forwarded the message to ten friends.

items.e: To suspend something is to stop it for a while, which is what umpires do when lightning arrives; extending, announcing, or repeating the game would all keep it going. Suspend can also mean to hang something up.
items.q: The umpires had to ______ the game in the fourth inning, and both teams waited under the bleachers until the lightning had passed.

items.e: A sanctuary is a safe place where something is protected, which is what a refuge for hurt birds is; a laboratory is for experiments, a boundary is a line, and a predicament is a situation rather than a place.
items.q: The injured owl was carried to a bird ______ outside town, where volunteers fed it by hand until it was strong enough to hunt again.

items.e: A trace is the tiny amount left behind, so “not a trace” means none at all, which fits grass that is green and dry from end to end. Trace can also mean to copy a drawing through thin paper.
items.q: By noon there was not a ______ of snow left on the field; the grass was green and dry from one end to the other.

items.e: To suspect is to start believing something is true before you have proof, which is what the missing sandwiches lead Dad to think about the puppy; he is not telling anyone, he is far from certain, and he plainly has not forgotten.
items.q: After the third sandwich went missing from the counter, Dad began to ______ that the new puppy was not as innocent as she looked.
